title: Never Outshine the Master
summary: Brilliance in the presence of a superior is not a gift. It is a threat, and it will be priced accordingly.
core: The law asserts that in any hierarchy, superiority is a kind of danger. A superior made to look foolish will either set the subordinate aside or remove him, and both outcomes cost the subordinate more than deference ever would. The reasoning rests on an asymmetry: the person above controls pay, title, access, and the account of who caused what, while talent can be reassigned or quietly ignored. The judgement implied is unflattering. Talent displayed before a superior is not evidence of virtue but of a failure to read the room. The useful posture is to appear valuable, deferential, and slightly less luminous than the person whose position is wanted. There is also a warning about time. Even the genuinely indispensable eventually become merely tolerated.
observance: When the law is followed, the superior's self-regard is left intact and the subordinate survives. Ptolemy I Soter offers the cleanest case. Having served as one of Alexander the Great's generals and succeeded him in Egypt, Ptolemy built the Library at Alexandria and attached Alexander's name to it, so credit for the new ruler flowed backward to the dead conqueror rather than forward to the living one. Alexander kept the glory and Ptolemy kept the position. Cosimo de' Medici, returning from exile to Florence in 1434, entered in plain robes, preserved the forms of the republic, and governed the city for three decades without accepting a crown. Men who never made their master feel small were the men still there when the succession came.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the subordinate becomes a problem the institution must solve. Cardinal Richelieu was Louis XIII's chief minister from 1624 and by nearly every measure the abler of the two. He rebuilt the royal army, dismantled the private strongholds of the great nobles, and became the visible author of French revival, which implicitly reduced a young king of weak reputation to a figurehead. The overreach came to a head in November 1630 in the Day of the Dupes, when Marie de' Medici and the leading peers moved to have the cardinal dismissed. Louis XIII wavered, then chose his minister, and Richelieu was saved only by exile and by the king's death shortly after. The inference drawn by his enemies was blunt: a minister who makes the crown look weak has become a rival to the crown.
reversal: The law describes frightened people rather than a law of nature, and it fails in two directions. A superior who punishes subordinates for excellence is left with no competent people, which is how courts and companies rot from within. Alexander the Great was killed by his own officers rather than by a Persian. The caution applies below as well. Silence that reads as incompetence cannot be told apart from silence caused by weakness, and hiding capability indefinitely caps the ceiling as surely as it flatters. The workable posture is calibration rather than concealment. Make the superior look capable in front of others, keep the subordinate's own competence legible to the record, and choose the room in which to display it.

title: Never put too Much Trust in Friends, Learn how to use Enemies
summary: A friend has no reason to stay loyal when loyalty becomes costly. An enemy has every reason to prove himself.
core: The law draws a distinction between affection and leverage. Friendship is entered voluntarily, has no binding structure, and dissolves exactly when it becomes inconvenient. Hostility is the opposite, and it imposes an obligation. An opponent who changes sides must demonstrate the change, and that demonstration buys gratitude affection never can. The reasoning also concerns information. Friends tell what flatters them; enemies tell what actually happened, because they have a motive to make the position of others worse. The judgement implied is cold. Sentiment is not a security arrangement, and the person who relies on it is not loyal but merely unchallenged. The conclusion is not to manufacture enemies but to stop treating an adversary as a spent resource.
observance: When the law is followed, the survivor is the one who never confused approval with alliance. Charles Maurice de Talleyrand is the standard illustration, if a morally uncomfortable one. Born in 1754 into an aristocratic family that had fallen out of favour, he held office under Louis XVI, worked through the Revolution, served as foreign minister under Napoleon, negotiated the restoration of Louis XVIII at the Congress of Vienna, and was still a central figure under Louis-Philippe. Each regime he served would have regarded him as a traitor. Talleyrand did not regard himself as one. He treated every government as a temporary employer and kept his position by being indispensable to whoever was ascending rather than loyal to whoever had fallen.
transgression: When the law is ignored, dependence is placed on people who feel no obligation to supply it. Thomas Cromwell served Henry VIII for a decade as a competent lawyer and an effective minister, and the king came to rely on him absolutely on matters ranging from the royal succession to the reform of the English church. His position rested on being irreplaceable in the king's eyes and on a conviction that his own advancement and the crown's interests were the same thing. When Henry's marital plans shifted, that conviction became the whole of his danger. Cromwell was summoned to a council meeting in the summer of 1540, arrested as he sat, and beheaded days later without trial. No friend warned him, because he had surrounded himself with men who owed him.
reversal: An enemy who has been converted is loyal for a reason that expires. The obligation is to demonstrate worthiness, and once that has been done and the former adversary installed, the incentive disappears. Talleyrand is the standing warning: a man who served Louis XVI, the Revolution, Napoleon, the Restoration and Louis-Philippe outlived every one of them, and by 1830 he was a relic, mocked as the archetype of treachery. The reverse holds for friends. Loyalty freely given can be withdrawn freely, and affection is no substitute for obligation. Expect too much gratitude from a converted opponent and the discovery will come at the worst moment: usefulness has run out ahead of position.

title: Conceal Your Intentions
summary: The moment an intention becomes readable, it stops belonging to the person who formed it.
core: The law asserts that an intention is a weapon only while it is private. Once an adversary can name the objective, the objective stops belonging to its author and becomes a problem to be solved: markets move, alliances firm, and fortifications are repaired before the attacker arrives. Concealment is therefore not cowardice but timing. The method is to make intent and action non-consecutive, so that commitment arrives as a surprise rather than as confirmation. The reasoning is also about the social cost of explanation. A stated intention invites negotiation, objection and coalition-building, all of which give the other side time and allies. The judgement implied is that candour is a luxury available only to those already strong. Open plans read as either aggression or incompetence.
observance: When the law is followed, the opponent is still arguing about the wrong campaign when the blow lands. In the spring of 1796 a young French commander took command in Italy and began the campaign that made him a national figure. Napoleon Bonaparte was careful to disperse his forces across the Ligurian coast rather than mass them, so that Austrian observers, who knew an army was somewhere in the region, could not determine where it would strike. The Austrians were not merely surprised by the direction; they were uncertain whether there was a direction at all until it had already been committed. The French then moved faster than the dispatches describing them, and the same methods were used repeatedly through the campaign.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the other side does not have to guess, and bluff becomes unnecessary because there is nothing hidden to detect. Adolf Hitler published the general shape of his intentions against the Soviet Union in Mein Kampf years before carrying them out, including the argument that Germany's future lay in the east. The specifics leaked as well. British intelligence had a good working estimate of the German deployment and timetable before the invasion of the Soviet Union began on 22 June 1941, and Churchill's warnings to Stalin that month were largely discounted. Concealment is not only about words. It is about the movement of troops, the traffic through cipher machines, and the pattern visible to anyone paying attention.
reversal: Concealment has a cost that is easy to underestimate. An intention nobody can read is also one nobody can cooperate with, and an organisation held in ignorance of the objective will supply it badly or supply it late. The longer intent is kept private, the more brittle the moment of disclosure, because a plan that surprises everyone also surprises the people carrying it out. There is a further cost in the psychology of the concealed. Ambiguity sustained over months stops feeling like strategy and starts to feel like isolation, and an isolated strategist makes errors of judgement that a candid one would have had corrected by colleagues. The workable discipline is narrow: conceal the destination, not the intent among one's own people.

title: Always Say Less than Necessary
summary: Every additional word is another chance to say the one thing that undoes everything else.
core: The law asserts that speech is the most common way people destroy advantages they were otherwise born with. Each sentence widens the area of what can be quoted, analysed, or regretted, and the risk lives in the marginal sentence, since the first ones are the ones the speaker rehearsed. Restraint also has a mechanical effect on others. Someone who finishes early leaves the room having to fill the space with speculation, and speculation is not controllable. The reasoning treats language as a resource to be spent rather than poured. The judgement implied is unkind and largely accurate. Most people speak not because they have something to add but because silence feels like weakness, and the fear of seeming ordinary supplies the word that ends them. Composure, not vocabulary, registers as authority.
observance: When the law is followed, the speaker stays in control because there is nothing to seize on. The clearest modern case is Bill Clinton before the federal grand jury in August 1998, testifying about the Lewinsky matter. Advised by his lawyers to say as little as possible, he largely did, answering the central question with a narrow denial that he had not had sexual relations with the woman named and otherwise deflecting to the irrelevance of the specific questions put to him. The discipline held through several days of testimony and through the televised address that followed, when he admitted the affair while declining to elaborate on it. Nothing further was admitted, and the administration survived the year intact.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the speaker supplies the opposition with evidence at no cost. Prince Charles demonstrated this in 1976, when a speech he delivered at Harvard to mark the university's bicentenary was leaked in full, including an extended passage in a mock-solemn register about a sleeping bear, red-hot sleepers, and the trappings of American student life. The tone collapsed under transcription. The same failure recurred more damagingly in 1992, when a telephone conversation between Charles and his companion was recorded without either of them knowing and was published verbatim, damaging a reputation he had spent decades defending. In both cases the content was ordinary. The exposure was the entire consequence of having said, and recorded, more than was required.
reversal: Restraint is only power when the audience believes it is deliberate. Silence that reads as fear, incompetence or evasion cannot be told apart from silence caused by those things, and in a negotiation the first person to speak convincingly usually sets the terms. The law also fails against adversaries who will not stop, since there are people who fill a silence themselves, construct the position for you, and let the record show that the question went unanswered. The workable discipline is not muteness. Decide in advance what is worth having repeated, answer the answerable version of the question first and at a normal speed, and accept that a refusal will be quoted exactly as often as a detail would have been.

title: So Much Depends on Reputation - Guard it with your Life
summary: Reputation is the currency power actually moves in. It is slow to earn and instant to lose.
core: The law asserts that power is not held directly but granted by the judgement of others, and that this judgement admits no appeal. Character, competence and reliability are not consulted separately; they are averaged into a single number determining who is trusted with anything consequential. The reasoning follows from the trust problem. Whoever cannot observe an intention must substitute a prediction, and reputation is that prediction. This makes reputation the cheapest and most concentrated form of collateral a person can hold. The judgement implied is that character is an asset to be managed rather than a private condition, and that a man who assumes his integrity is self-evident has mistaken a private fact for a public one. Reputation is also fragile in a specific way: built slowly from many small confirmations, destroyed by the one that contradicts them.
observance: When the law is followed, the reputation does the work that persuasion would otherwise have to. Elizabeth I is the model. Throughout her reign she was presented, and largely presented herself, as Gloriana, the Virgin Queen: modest, chaste, Protestant, standing outside faction, with the image managed through royal portraiture, through staged progresses, and through a cultivated literary cult around her person. The policy paid off at the point of greatest stress. After her death in 1603 the crowds at her tomb in Westminster Abbey were unprecedented, an outpouring of grief with immediate political value for the successor. The reign had produced wars, executions, and religious division. The surviving judgement was of a monarch who had held a court together and had been owed something at the end.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the collapse is sudden and total because everything was resting on the one thing. Richard Nixon entered the presidency with a reputation for political skill built over two decades and spent it in four years. The Watergate burglary in 1972 was mishandled, then covered, then lied about under oath. The unraveling was driven less by the break-in than by the insistence on managing the story: the dismissal of the special prosecutor in 1973, the tapes, and the emergence of a second scandal concerning the cover itself. The House Judiciary Committee voted articles of impeachment on 27 July 1974 and he resigned on 9 August. He survived in politics for three more decades, but the reputation was never recoverable.
reversal: Reputation is an asset with a very asymmetric price, and the commonest error is over-weighting it. A reputation maintained by avoidance eventually becomes a reputation for nothing in particular, which leaves its holder protected from scandal and equally protected from opportunity. There is a failure mode in which the reputation itself becomes the target. Marie Antoinette, whose Austrian birth and foreign connections were used against her for years, found that the image of a foreign woman at the centre of French court had hardened into evidence against itself, and she could not answer a charge about her nationality because that was the charge. Reputation is a contested description of a person, and its strictest auditor is rarely its author.

title: Court Attention at all Cost
summary: The person nobody notices has no power, however talented. Attention is the precondition of influence.
core: The law asserts that power requires an audience before it requires anything else, and that obscurity is a form of exile almost nobody chooses deliberately. The reasoning is structural. Decisions about resources, credit and advancement are made by people who must first know a candidate exists, and the unknown candidate is not a candidate. Attention also functions as proof: the number of people watching is taken as evidence of the thing being watched, which is why attention feeds itself. The judgement implied is that modesty, insofar as it is a strategy rather than a temperament, is usually a mistake, and that the wish to be left alone usually conceals a wish to be spared the effort of being noticed. Attention that must be manufactured becomes a performance of attention, and such audiences are fickle.
observance: When the law is followed, the person becomes legible before he becomes known, and the machinery of attention works for him. P. T. Barnum built an American reputation in the 1840s and 1850s through relentless publicity rather than through any singular achievement. He arranged to be announced in advance wherever he travelled, and in New York he hoisted flags on buildings to signal his arrival. The most systematic of his devices was the telegraph: he paid an operator to send reports of his shows and receipts to newspapers ahead of his own arrival, so the press had a story ready before it had a subject. Audiences arrived persuaded that something extraordinary was happening, which is to say already believing. Barnum understood that being asked for is the second condition of influence, and he supplied it first.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the work goes on and the career does not. Emily Dickinson wrote nearly eighteen hundred poems, kept them, and published roughly ten of them during her lifetime. She circulated them in deliberately private handwriting rather than in print, which guaranteed the outcome. The consequence was that almost nobody knew the work existed. Her poems were not collected and published in volume until after her death in 1886, and the substantial editions came decades later, by which time the reputation they established belonged to a writer nobody had heard of. The tragedy is not that she failed to write. It is that she succeeded for six decades in a room with no window, and by the time the window was opened she had no audience left to build anything with.
reversal: Attention is an input, not a result, and it can be substituted for substance indefinitely until the substitution is tested. A reputation built entirely on spectacle collapses at first contact with someone who has read the work, and the collapse is worse than obscurity would have been, because a prior image now has to be disproved. The second failure is that visibility is a permanent liability as well as an asset. Elvis Presley received more attention than almost any performer of his century and spent the last years of his life under the constant gaze of a small group of handlers at a property in Memphis, largely unable to leave. Notice is dependency running in both directions.

title: Get others to do the Work for you, but Always Take the Credit
summary: Employ others to do the work, arrange for the credit, and it buys time without buying humility.
core: The law asserts that doing one's own work is the most expensive habit available to anyone with leverage. The reasoning is economic before it is moral. The person who performs the task is paid for the task and remains replaceable the moment it is completed; the person who directs and represents the outcome is paid for the judgement and remains in place as long as the results keep arriving. Delegation converts a scarce input, personal time, into an effectively unlimited one. Taking the credit is the part everyone objects to and rarely examines, because the record of an institution is written by those who summarise it rather than those who generate it. The judgement implied is that modesty in attribution is a luxury of the unprotected.
observance: When the law is followed, the institution grows faster than the individual can, and the individual remains its public face. Louis XIV is the clearest case in modern European history. He governed an expanding administration for seventy-two years and personally directed very little of it. Finance was run by Colbert, who rebuilt the tax system, the manufactures, and the royal finances. Fortifications were run by Vauban, whose sieges across Europe were carried out by other men and credited to the king. The decorative programme of Versailles was run by Le Brun and his successors. The king took the credit for all of it, and the label became France itself. He was in no meaningful sense the author of the policy, which is precisely why the credit was available for him to hold.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the arrangement inverts and the person who does the work ends up with nothing. Ub Iwerks, Walt Disney's earliest partner and the artist who designed and built the characters of the early shorts, including the design of Mickey Mouse, left the studio in 1930 after disputes over pay and recognition. He carried the idea of a new character to a competitor, and within a year the rivals had a film closely resembling Disney's own productions, which pushed Disney toward the same invention. Iwerks returned to Disney in 1940 and worked there again for sixteen years, but he never held the public authorship of the work he had made. He was honoured only late, and he died in 1971 while the public account of the studio's history continued without him.
reversal: The credit system works only while the record can be controlled, and it collapses when the record belongs to someone else. Ub Iwerks is the demonstration. He left, built his own studio, and put the substance of the invention into a competitor's hands; within a year the rival studio had a film close to Mickey Mouse, and Disney's response was to make the same invention and hold the public credit for it. That is how the arrangement appeared from outside, and it is why the accusation followed him. The general failure is accumulated resentment. People who did the work without the credit talk to one another, and a profession systematically under-credited eventually produces a historian. And a person who takes credit cannot inspect the work.

title: Make other People come to you - use Bait if Necessary
summary: A person who is sought after controls the terms of the meeting before the meeting has begun.
core: The law asserts that whoever initiates a negotiation has already conceded something, even when he appears to be the one asking. Whoever must travel, wait or petition is subordinate during the interval, and the interval is where positions get set. The arrangement of a meeting is therefore itself a strategy, and the ability to refuse to move is a resource. The law goes on to the commoner case, where the more powerful party does not yet have anything worth travelling for. Bait is the answer: a visible sign that something is available, offered without effort, so that interest forms in the other party and the obligation to approach reverses. Eagerness is a disclosure. A person who shows need has told the room what can be extracted, and no later skill fully recovers that ground.
observance: When the law is followed, the powerful party waits and the others come. In 1981 the French president Charles de Gaulle, isolated in his own camp and challenged from within it, invited a group of leading men of the opposing political tendency to a single dinner at his country house in Sologne. The occasion was reported widely enough that declining would have required a public explanation. What followed was a long negotiation over a subsequent change of government in which the guests participated and the president, by most accounts, largely set the terms. He had made no speech and advanced no programme. He had supplied the circumstance, and they had supplied the attendance, which is the entire method: the more powerful man arranged the conditions under which seeking his favour became easier than refusing it.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the supplicant travels and the journey itself becomes the argument. Christopher Columbus spent roughly eight years attempting to obtain backing for a westward voyage, presenting his proposal to the courts and commercial houses of Portugal and to the court of Castile through intermediaries. Much of that time was spent being deferred to. The matter was examined at length by councils that recommended postponement, and the objections raised, on grounds of geography and of the authority required for such an undertaking, were not absurd. When backing finally came from Isabella of Castile in 1486, the expedition set out under terms largely unfavourable to him. On his return he found the granting administration changed and the terms of his governorship altered against him, and he came home in custody.
reversal: The strategy fails whenever the invitation is not in fact an invitation. A man who summons rivals to dinner in order to frighten them has told them both what he fears and where he is. Talleyrand, who held open dinners to which diplomats of every faction came and whose career ran from Louis XVI through Napoleon to Louis-Philippe, understood what that arrangement cost: by the end he was owed nothing by anyone, which is exactly the condition under which such a room stops working. There is a second failure in the bait itself, since a manufactured sign of availability will be tested, and if what is delivered does not match the promise the cost is the credibility required for the next attempt.

title: Win through your Actions, Never through Argument
summary: An argument ends when the room empties. A result changes what the room believes is possible.
core: The law asserts that debate settles nothing and that victory in a contest of speeches is indistinguishable from defeat. Argument has a structure that makes it unreliable: the more a claim is defended, the more it becomes a matter of identity for the defender, and the exchange proceeds by counter rather than by inquiry. It also rewards volume, and volume is the property most easily possessed by the person with least to lose. Action reverses the terms. A delivered result is a fact about the world, and facts are not contested the way opinions are. The judgement implied is not that argument is worthless but that it is a tool for people who cannot yet act, and that continuing to use it afterwards is a habit of mind. A refusal to argue can also read as a refusal to account.
observance: When the law is followed, the dispute is settled by the world rather than by the speakers. Henry Ford's contest with the Detroit Automobile Company over the quadracyclic engine ended in the federal court in Detroit in 1903, and when the case went to the jury it took nine minutes to return. The verdict was for Ford and the company was ordered to pay. This was not a Ford that had argued better than its opponent. It was a Ford that had assembled a better engine, a better demonstration, and the better prepared case, and then allowed the machinery to speak. The doctrine behind the law is unglamorous and old. Put something into the world that makes the argument obsolete, and the argument will be dropped by people who have better things to do.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the argument becomes the work, and the argument is won by the wrong person. In 1858 Abraham Lincoln agreed to debate Stephen Douglas in a series of joint appearances across Illinois. Lincoln took the engagement expecting to lose and said as much in advance, telling his associates that he did not think he could beat Douglas in argument but that Douglas might be damaged politically by the exposure. The prediction was accurate in its consequences and in its author. The debates made Douglas a national figure and established him as the leading statesman of the West, and for a period the country's future seemed to turn on a rivalry between two men in an Illinois courthouse. Lincoln's eventual victory came two years later, from organisation and from the realignment the debate had accelerated.
reversal: The law fails in both directions, and both failures are common. Toward those who cannot be moved by a result, argument is not merely inferior but necessary; a person who refuses to make the case in words will be described to others as having nothing to say, and that account will be written by the opponent. Toward those already persuaded, action is wasted effort, because the commitment was never in question and only timing was. There is also a cost in the public posture. Repeated action without explanation is easily read as evasion, and Lincoln's presidency, which rested overwhelmingly on delivered results, was for years judged thin in doctrine. Act first, argue second, and argue only where the argument will be heard by those who decide.

title: Infection: Avoid the Unhappy and Unlucky
summary: Misfortune attaches to whomever stands nearest it. Choose the company deliberately.
core: The law asserts two things usually kept apart. The first is psychological: temperament and expectation are transmissible, and a person who spends his days among the aggrieved finds his own outlook narrowing to their range. The second is social: a person whose reputation is tied to a series of failures acquires a reputation for failure, and that judgement precedes any examination of the particulars. The reasoning is that circumstance is read as character by everyone not present for the explanation. The judgement implied is severe and easily misunderstood. The conclusion is not that the unsuccessful are worthless but that association is a form of credit rating the associate neither consented to nor can audit. Constant proximity to disaster also narrows what is attempted, since expected return falls as perceived risk rises.
observance: When the law is followed, the household and the office are constructed to reduce the number of catastrophes that can reach the person at the centre. Franklin D. Roosevelt is the most thoroughly documented case. The inner circle around him was cultivated rather than inherited, and its members understood that part of their work was managing what reached him and when. Reporters and political opponents were handled so consistently that the press rarely obtained access to him directly, and much of what the public saw was shaped by a small number of intermediaries selected partly for their buoyancy. The result was a public figure whose visible condition was steady confidence, which is itself a strategic asset, because it reads as competence whether or not the underlying position was secure.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the association becomes the explanation and the explanation becomes the outcome. Edward II of England placed almost all his authority in a small group of favourites, chiefly Hugh Despenser the Younger and Hugh Despenser the Elder, and allowed them to absorb access to the crown. The extent of that dependence became notorious and was catalogued in detail, most fully in the Kirkstall Psalter, which listed the king's companions as though they were his household officers. Isabella of France and Roger Mortimer crossed to England in 1326, and what followed was not a defeat in argument but the removal of the person. Edward was deposed and confined. His company had made the transfer of power legible and inevitable.
reversal: The law mistakes correlation for cause and is dangerous in the hands of anyone who believes it literally. It is not that unlucky people are contagious. It is that the people around a person who is losing tend to be losing with him, and the arrow more often runs downstream than the law allows. Machiavelli's advice to princes is closer to the truth: a ruler should learn how not to be by imagining misfortune rather than by choosing less unlucky company, because fortune cannot be quarantined. There is a moral cost as well. A circle assembled for the suppression of bad news produces a leader who is never corrected, and the correction arrives late and from outside.

title: Learn to Keep People Dependent on You
summary: Dependence is the quietest form of control. Never be one of two sources where one will do.
core: The law asserts that the strongest authority is not persuasion but indispensability. A person who controls the only route to a necessary thing does not need to win arguments, because the structure has already settled them. The reasoning is an account of behaviour under scarcity. Where there is an alternative supplier, the customer has a price and an opinion. Where there is not, the customer has only a judgement about quality, and judgement can be shaped by whoever has been supplying the goods. The judgement implied is that autonomy is expensive and should be given away carefully. It also implies something bleak about what power consists of: not dominating people but occupying the position in which other plans run through that judgement.
observance: When the law is followed, the relationship becomes difficult to leave, and it does so quietly. Karl Lagerfeld ran Chanel for roughly three decades from 1983 and made the house the dominant fashion institution of the period. He also built a structure in which the founder's dependence was absolute and unacknowledged. Lagerfeld handled her collections, decided what appeared on the runway, and was effectively the only person who could authorise a decision about the house itself. The ownership was not his. The house belonged to a family holding company, and he held no legal power over it. What he controlled was the entire apparatus through which any decision would have had to pass, and that is the form the dependence usually takes: not legal authority, but complete presence at every point where anything can be done.
transgression: When the law is ignored, the person becomes one of several rather than the only one, and the position must then be defended by persuasion. Leonardo da Vinci spent his last years in France at the invitation of Francis I and was given a generous allowance and a residence at the Clos Lucé in Amboise. He was never granted an appointment carrying authority, never given control of a project, and never given a pupil. He continued writing to patrons and intermediaries about his unfinished work, including the Treatise on Water, and he died at Clos Lucé in 1519 with no institution behind him and no one obliged to continue. He had made himself invaluable to a great many people across a career of extraordinary range, but never to the point where any single institution could not do without him.
reversal: Dependence is a contract, and contracts require the other party's continuing consent to be dependent. The moment that person works out what they would do if the supply stopped, the arrangement stops being a relationship and becomes a hostage situation. The obverse risk is that indispensability is recognised by everyone except the person who depends on it, and is therefore resented rather than relied upon. The structure is also more brittle than it appears: a single point of dependency is a single point of failure, and a position built on monopolising an indispensable role can be ended at once by building anything at all beside it. Concentrate the value only as far as it can be replaced quickly.

title: Use Selective Honesty and Generosity to Disarm your Victim
summary: Total war is expensive. A concession offered at the right moment costs a fraction and disarms the rest.
core: The law asserts that open hostility is the most expensive weapon available, because it is the only one that invites the other side to spend without limit. It proposes a deliberate mixture instead, part truth and part concession, timed to arrive when the other party has already committed itself. The reasoning is about reciprocity. An opponent being fought will organise his whole identity around fighting. An opponent granted something small, in a way that cannot be returned and so must be accepted, is placed in the position of a person who has received something and cannot attack the giver without appearing to reject it. The judgement implied is unsentimental. Total honesty exposes intention and supplies material for a coalition. Total severity converts one adversary into a class, and a class is harder to disarm than a person.
observance: When the law is followed, the opponent is rendered harmless by generosity he cannot categorise. Benjamin Franklin described in his Autobiography the circumstances of a feud with the printers of his brother's newspaper in Philadelphia. Rather than answer the attacks, he went to their establishments and received them personally, allowing the editors to say whatever they wished without resistance and then to observe that they were dealing with a person rather than an abstraction. The editors, having exhausted the material and received nothing to fight, became the men most likely to say publicly that they had been wrong. The same method appears in his handling of a slight from a member of the Pennsylvania assembly, where he wrote first and received the apology he sought. The concession was not an admission.
transgression: When the law is ignored, hostility produces a person with nothing left to lose. Caracalla came to the purple in 211 as a boy of twelve alongside his brother Geta, and the two were immediately at odds. In 212 he had Geta murdered, and the ancient accounts record that the killing was arranged to occur at a family meeting attended by their mother Julia Domna. Geta was killed at her feet. Julia Domna then became, in effect, the last surviving member of the imperial family, and she had no tribunal to appeal to inside it. Within four years she was dead, by his arrangements. There was no generosity anywhere in the method, only the refusal to consider one, and nothing was ever disarmed by it.
reversal: The law fails in the presence of someone who has already been disarmed twice. Elizabeth I pardoned Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, after his rising of 1601, and had pardoned him after his part in the rising of 1589 as well. Both times she had the power to end him and did not. Her forgiveness therefore carried no information, because it had been shown not to mean anything, and Devereux returned to conspiracy and died in the Tower of London preparing another attempt. Generosity disarms only while it is rare and while the recipient understands why it was extended. And a concession granted to prevent an attack teaches everyone watching what the price of attacking is.
